sequences.title: Food & Café: The Magic Ordering Phrase

screens.title: You already speak café
lines: Croissant, chocolat, menu — French gave English half of its food words, so you arrive with a head start.
Today you learn the spell that turns those words into actual snacks: je voudrais.

vocab.meaning: I would like — the polite ordering phrase
please (polite — to a waiter or any adult)
and — for ordering two things at once

screens.framing: No grade, no pressure — guess with your gut. French food words are English's cousins.

screens.title: Two tiny verbs run your whole weekend
lines: Knitting, baking, reading, K-pop — you already HAVE the hobbies; French just needs the verbs.
Meet faire (to do), jouer (to play) and aller (to go): three little engines that describe almost any weekend.

vocab.meaning: to do an activity — je fais du tricot (I knit)
to play a sport or game — je joue au foot
to go — je vais au parc (I go to the park)

screens.title: Numbers wearing a tiny clock hat
lines: Great news: you already own French numbers, and telling time is just numbers plus the word heures.
One question runs every clock in France: Quelle heure est-il?

items.prompt: Let's order at the café together — the full polite combo, start to finish.

steps.text: Rule one: greet before you order. 'Bonjour!' opens every café door in France — skipping it is considered quite rude.
The magic phrase: Je voudrais… = I would like… It orders ANYTHING: Je voudrais un croissant. Je voudrais un thé.

check.question: Your friend wants cake. What should they say?

steps.text: Want two things? Join them with et (and): 'Je voudrais un croissant ET un chocolat chaud.' One bonjour, two treats.
Seal it with s'il vous plaît (please): 'Bonjour! Je voudrais un croissant et un chocolat chaud, s'il vous plaît.'

steps.text: The waiter returns: 'Voilà!' You answer 'Merci!' — and that is a complete café mission. 🥐

items.prompt: Saying what you do: faire for activities, jouer for games, aller for going places.

steps.text: faire = to do: je fais (I do), tu fais (you do). Activities use faire de — Je fais du tricot = I knit, literally 'I do some knitting'.
More faire de hobbies: je fais de la pâtisserie (I bake), je fais de la natation (I swim), je fais de la danse (I dance).
Sports and games you PLAY take jouer à instead: je joue au foot (soccer), je joue aux cartes (cards).
Going places is aller: je vais, tu vas, on va. Je vais au parc = I'm going to the park.

items.prompt: Telling time like a Parisian — one question, one pattern, two VIP words.

steps.text: The question: Quelle heure est-il? (What time is it?) The answer ALWAYS begins the same way: Il est… (It is…).
Il est trois heures = it's 3 o'clock. Swap in any number you already know: il est huit heures = 8:00.
Add-ons: et quart = quarter past (:15), et demie = half past (:30), moins le quart = quarter TO (:45). Il est trois heures et demie = 3:30.
Careful — moins le quart leans on the NEXT hour: il est quatre heures moins le quart = 3:45 (a quarter taken AWAY from 4).

check.question: Il est neuf heures moins le quart — what time is it?

steps.text: Two VIP times skip numbers entirely: midi (noon) and minuit (midnight). Il est midi — lunchtime across all of France.

items.prompt: Finish the clock readings.

lines: 3:00 → Il est trois [[heures]].
3:30 → Il est trois heures et [[demie]].

items.hint: heures = o'clock; the half-past word is demie.
items.explanation: Il est + number + heures, then et demie bolts the half hour on.

items.prompt: Now the tricky ones — quarters and a VIP hour.

lines: 7:15 → Il est sept heures et [[quart]].
8:45 → Il est neuf heures [[moins]] le quart.
Noon → Il est [[midi]].

items.hint: 8:45 leans forward onto 9 — that's the moins move. And noon needs no number at all.
items.explanation: et quart adds 15, moins le quart borrows from the next hour, and midi stands proudly alone.

items.prompt: A passerby asks: 'Quelle heure est-il?' What do they want to know?

items.explanation: Quelle heure est-il? = What time is it? The answer always starts with Il est…

items.prompt: Où est le chat? Learn the rooms, then hunt the house cat with five tiny position words.

steps.text: Meet the rooms: la cuisine (kitchen), la chambre (bedroom), le salon (living room), la salle de bains (bathroom), le jardin (garden).
Somewhere in this house, a cat is hiding. The question that finds him: Où est le chat? = Where is the cat?
Five position words crack every hiding spot: sur (on), sous (under), dans (in), devant (in front of), derrière (behind).
Le chat est sur le lit (on the bed). Le chat est sous la table (under the table). Le chat est dans le jardin (in the garden). He gets around.
